chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from one of his companions, from Abu Baseer, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), regarding

a man who fractured another man, exposing the bone. Then he sought (forgiveness) so he gifted it to him. Then it worsened, so it killed him. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'He is responsible for the wergild except for the price of the exposed bone, because he had gifted it to him, and he had not gifted the self.'
And regarding the Simhaq (cut reaching the bone but less than exposure), it is five hundred Dirhams.
And regarding it, if it is in the face, it is double the wergild according to the degree of shame (it causes).

And regarding the Ma'mumah (skull fracture), it is a third of the wergild. And it is that which has penetrated but has not reached the cavity (of the brain), so it is what is between the two (exposure and Simhaq).
And regarding the Ja'ifah (piercing), it is a third of the wergild. And it is that which has reached the cavity of the brain.
And regarding the Munqiliah (bone displacement), it is fifteen camels. And it is that which has become a wound from which the bones are displaced.

key_terms.الدِّيَة: The wergild or blood money paid for injury or death
key_terms.الشَّيْن: Shame or disgrace, used here to measure the severity of facial injuries
key_terms.جَائِفَة: An injury that has reached the cavity of the brain
key_terms.سَمْحَاق: An injury that reaches the bone but does not expose it
key_terms.مَأْمُومَة: A skull fracture that has penetrated but not reached the brain cavity
key_terms.مُنَقِّلَة: An injury causing displacement of the bones
key_terms.مُوضِحَة: An injury that exposes the bone

ai.seo_question: What are the specific diyah (blood money) amounts for different types of bone fractures and head injuries in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elaborates on the jurisprudential nuances of *diyah* (blood money) for head injuries, specifically distinguishing between *al-mudhihah* (exposing the bone) and *al-simhaq* (a lesser wound). It highlights the principle that a gift of the wound does not equate to a gift of the life, as illustrated by the case where the victim died after the wound reopened, thereby clarifying the liability for compensation based on the depth of penetration and the specific anatomical structures affected.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from one of his comapnions, from Abu Baseer,

(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> regarding a man who fractured a man exposing his bone. Then he sought (forgiveness) so he gifted it to him. Then it (injury) worsened, so it killed him. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘He is responsible for the wergild except for the price of the bone exposed, because he had gifted it to him, and he had not gifted the self;
and regarding the cut which reaches the bone, and it is less than the exposure, being of five hundred Dirhams,
and with regards to it when it was in the face, it would be double the wergild upon the measurement of the shame (it caused);
and regarding the skull fracture being a third of the wergild, and it is which had been plunged in and did not reach to the middle, so it is regarding what is between the two;
and regarding the piercing of the hole is a third of the wergild, and it is which had reached the middle of the brain;
and regarding the bone displacement being fifteen from the camels, and it is which had become a blister, the bone being displaced from it’.
